<div class="learn-box">
**What you will learn**

Choose a table shape for your question and run one small example of every format, including explicit survival censoring.
</div>

**You need:** the client packages and the Opal login from
[Getting started](book-00-start.html). This chapter uses `omop.synthea`, the
public synthetic Synthea27Nj data.

## Start this chapter

Log in first:




``` r
library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.synthea", server = "site")$conns
```



The connection is ready; `conns` identifies the server used by the analysis calls.

## Choose the shape for the analysis

An output controls the shape of a private server table. It never grants a row
download. *Grain* means what one row represents: a person, an indexed episode,
an event or a time period. More rows do not create more independent people.

| Format | Use it for | Main row meaning |
|---|---|---|
| wide | A few named variables, models | Person or episode |
| long | Event sequences | Event within a population episode |
| features | A feature table preset | Wide person or episode |
| baseline | Entry characteristics preset | Wide person or episode |
| person_period / panel | Repeated measurements over follow-up | Episode and time bin |
| temporal_covariates | Sparse changes over time | Nonzero covariate and time bin |
| survival | Time until an outcome or censoring | Follow-up record |
| intervals | Exposure or event spans | Interval |
| sparse | Many mostly absent covariates | Nonzero covariate |
| membership | Reuse population episodes | Population member episode |
| dictionary | Describe concepts used by outputs | Vocabulary entry |
| joined | Combine compatible private outputs | Declared join grain |

`features` and `baseline` are wide-table presets selected with `type`.
Use `format` to request the other shapes.

## Prepare one small study

We will reuse these definitions to compare output shapes. For the baseline
example we will also restrict the variables to information available at entry.
[Chapter 4](book-04-vocabulary.html) identifies Inpatient Visit (**9201**),
Outpatient Visit (**9202**), blood hemoglobin (**3000963**) and its g/dL unit
(**8713**).


``` r
visits <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = c(9201L, 9202L), name = "visits")
spans <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = c(9201L, 9202L), name = "spans")
inpatient <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = 9201L, name = "inpatient")
visitors <- omop_population("visitors", index = omop_index(visits))
```

Each first visit begins one episode. A later inpatient visit will be our outcome.


``` r
study_variables <- list(
  visits = omop_variable(event = visits, reducer = omop_reduce("count")),
  age = omop_age_at("index"),
  hemoglobin = omop_mean_value("measurement", 3000963L, unit = 8713L,
    window = omop_window(NULL, NULL)))
base <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = study_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("wide", rows = "visitors", format = "wide"))
```

The count and hemoglobin mean use all history to illustrate shapes. They are
not baseline covariates: a baseline analysis must restrict them to entry or
before. Age is completed age at the first visit.

## Wide: named columns


``` r
wide_result <- recipe_execute(base, out = c(wide = "D_fmt_wide"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_wide", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_wide in site`
#> [1] 28  6
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_wide in combined studies`
#> [1] 28  6
```

There are 28 rows, one per first-visit episode, and one column per requested variable. A person's
pseudonym and episode keys are supplied by the server.

## Long: keep event records

Use long when event order and repeated records matter. Select a named source instead of reducing it.


``` r
long <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = study_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("long", rows = "visitors", format = "long",
  sources = "visits"))
recipe_execute(long, out = c(long = "D_fmt_long"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_long", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_long in site`
#> [1] 1735    9
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_long in combined studies`
#> [1] 1735    9
```

The long output has 1,735 rows, one per selected visit. Its columns include
`concept_id` and `start_date`. Dates default to offsets from the index. One source makes the event-row meaning clear; multiple sources need an explicit event-log design.


``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_fmt_long$concept_id",
  useNA = "no", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
```

```
#> D_fmt_long$concept_id
#>  Inpatient_Visit Outpatient_Visit 
#>               13             1722
```

The 13 inpatient and 1,722 outpatient visits sum to 1,735 records. These are
visits by setting, rather than numbers of people. A person
may contribute many visits to either setting.

## Features: a wide preset

Use the features preset when a downstream analysis expects a feature table. Native typed variables preserve their declared values.


``` r
features <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = study_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("features", rows = "visitors", type = "features"))
recipe_execute(features, out = c(features = "D_fmt_features"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_features", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_features in site`
#> [1] 28  6
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_features in combined studies`
#> [1] 28  6
```

The features table has 28 rows, one per visitor, with the same values as wide.

## Baseline: characteristics at entry

Use baseline to name an entry-characteristics table. Define the time windows of its variables explicitly.


``` r
baseline_variables <- list(
  visits = omop_count("visit_occurrence", window = omop_window(-365, 0)),
  age = omop_age_at("index"),
  hemoglobin = omop_value_at_index("measurement", 3000963L,
    tolerance = c(-90, 0), unit = 8713L))
baseline <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = baseline_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("baseline", rows = "visitors", type = "baseline"))
recipe_execute(baseline, out = c(baseline = "D_fmt_baseline"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_baseline", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_baseline in site`
#> [1] 28  6
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_baseline in combined studies`
#> [1] 28  6
```

The baseline preset also has 28 rows. Here we explicitly changed the variables
to a visit count during days −365 to 0 and hemoglobin closest to entry within
days −90 to 0. The preset itself neither restricts all-history values nor bands
age; the variable definitions make these entry characteristics.

## Panels: one row per follow-up bin

A *bin* is a time interval. These are three 30-day bins after entry, not calendar months.


``` r
panel <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = study_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("panel", rows = "visitors", format = "person_period",
  options = list(sources = list(visits), bins = list(width = 30L),
    window = omop_window(1, 90), analyses = "count", representation = "dense")))
recipe_execute(panel, out = c(panel = "D_fmt_panel"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_panel", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_panel in site`
#> [1] 84  8
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_panel in combined studies`
#> [1] 84  8
```

The panel has 84 rows: 28 visitors × three bins. A dense panel retains empty
bins with zero event counts. `bins = list(calendar = "month")` instead aligns to calendar months, whose lengths vary. Account for repeated rows per person in downstream analysis.


``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_fmt_panel$visits_outpatient_visit_count",
  datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 84
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>        5%       10%       25%       50%       75%       90%       95%      Mean 
#> 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000 1.0000000 1.0000000 0.1904762
```

The mean is 0.19 outpatient visits per person and 30-day bin, and the median
is zero across 84 bins. Zero bins
remain in the denominator; a mean per bin is different from an all-history
visit count per person.

## Temporal covariates: sparse time bins

Use temporal covariates when you need nonzero covariate values with a time index. Including day zero gives this example actual nonzero entries.


``` r
temporal <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = study_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("temporal", rows = "visitors", format = "temporal_covariates",
  options = list(sources = list(visits), bin_width = 30L,
    window = omop_window(0, 89), analyses = "count")))
temporal_result <- recipe_execute(temporal, out = c(temporal = "D_fmt_temporal"), datasources = conns)
DSI::datashield.symbols(conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> [1] "D_fmt_baseline"              "D_fmt_features"             
#> [3] "D_fmt_long"                  "D_fmt_panel"                
#> [5] "D_fmt_temporal"              "D_fmt_temporal.covariateRef"
#> [7] "D_fmt_temporal.timeRef"      "D_fmt_wide"                 
#> [9] "omop"
```

``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_temporal", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_temporal in site`
#> [1] 36  6
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_temporal in combined studies`
#> [1] 36  6
```

The server now also holds `D_fmt_temporal.covariateRef` and `D_fmt_temporal.timeRef`.
The 36 rows count nonzero covariate/bin entries rather than people.
Keep the covariate and time reference tables with this result: their
keys need those definitions. Missing records and missing measurements are not automatically interchangeable.

## Survival: state the censoring rule

A *time-at-risk window* says when outcomes count. *Censoring* ends follow-up without recording the outcome. Here follow-up starts the day after entry and has no fixed upper limit.


``` r
survival <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = study_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("survival", rows = "visitors", format = "survival",
  options = list(outcomes = list(admission = inpatient),
    tar = omop_window(1, NULL), censor = list("observation_end", "death"))))
recipe_execute(survival, out = c(survival = "D_fmt_survival"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_survival", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_survival in site`
#> [1] 28  8
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_survival in combined studies`
#> [1] 28  8
```

The survival output has 28 rows, one per person for this single outcome.
Only the named censor sources cap follow-up: observation end and death here. The window also limits follow-up when its upper bound is finite. An episode end is not an extra censor unless requested. A censor is not a “no outcome ever” assertion. Always state the window: omitting it would use the default 730-day window.


``` r
survival_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_fmt_survival$event", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
survival_result$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
```

```
#> D_fmt_survival$event
#>  0  1 
#> 21  7
```

Seven people have `event = 1` (an observed admission); 21 have `event = 0`
(follow-up ended without an admission in the risk window).


``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_fmt_survival$follow_up_days", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>        5%       10%       25%       50%       75%       90%       95%      Mean 
#>   993.350  1913.500  3821.250  7462.000 14257.500 18489.000 21647.200  9291.571
```

Median follow-up is 7,462 days and the mean is 9,291.6 days. This spans much
of the simulated life histories because no upper time limit was imposed.
`follow_up_days` describes time observed until admission or censoring. Different
durations are why a survival analysis needs time as well as the event indicator.

## Intervals: keep a start and an end

Use intervals for recorded spans. These visit intervals have recorded start and end dates. The same layout can describe drug exposures or eras.


``` r
intervals <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = study_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("intervals", rows = "visitors", format = "intervals",
  options = list(sources = list(spans), window = omop_window(0, NULL))))
recipe_execute(intervals, out = c(intervals = "D_fmt_intervals"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_intervals", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_intervals in site`
#> [1] 1735    7
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_intervals in combined studies`
#> [1] 1735    7
```

The 1,735 interval rows represent recorded visit spans, with a start and an end.
Both bounds remain private, normally as index-relative days. Overlapping intervals are not automatically a union of covered days; define an era or a coverage reducer for that question.

## Sparse: nonzero covariates plus a reference

Use sparse for many covariates when most combinations have no contribution.


``` r
sparse <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = study_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("sparse", rows = "visitors", format = "sparse",
  options = list(sources = list(visits), analyses = c("binary", "count"))))
sparse_result <- recipe_execute(sparse, out = c(sparse = "D_fmt_sparse"), datasources = conns)
DSI::datashield.symbols(conns)
```

```
#> $site
#>  [1] "D_fmt_baseline"              "D_fmt_features"             
#>  [3] "D_fmt_intervals"             "D_fmt_long"                 
#>  [5] "D_fmt_panel"                 "D_fmt_sparse"               
#>  [7] "D_fmt_sparse.covariateRef"   "D_fmt_survival"             
#>  [9] "D_fmt_temporal"              "D_fmt_temporal.covariateRef"
#> [11] "D_fmt_temporal.timeRef"      "D_fmt_wide"                 
#> [13] "omop"
```

``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_sparse", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_sparse in site`
#> [1] 70  5
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_sparse in combined studies`
#> [1] 70  5
```

`D_fmt_sparse` comes with its reference table `D_fmt_sparse.covariateRef`.
The 70 sparse rows each hold a nonzero value for one person and covariate, so this
row count is not a population size. The data contain a covariate key and value. The reference companion maps keys to source, concept and analysis. A missing sparse row is not a missing person roster: retain membership separately. Each published patient component must meet its own support rule.

## Membership: retain the population roster

Use membership to keep entry/end dates and keys for every episode independently of its measurements.


``` r
membership <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits, spans, inpatient),
  populations = list(visitors), variables = study_variables,
  outputs = omop_output("membership", rows = "visitors", format = "membership"))
recipe_execute(membership, out = c(membership = "D_fmt_membership"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_membership", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_membership in site`
#> [1] 28  6
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_membership in combined studies`
#> [1] 28  6
```

The membership output has 28 rows, one for each first-visit episode.
This is still a patient-linked private object. It is not a public list of participants.

## Dictionary: describe the concepts

Use dictionary to describe vocabulary concepts used by a declared source output. Here `counts` defines those dependencies privately; only the dictionary is published. It does not contain patient rows.


``` r
dictionary <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits), populations = list(visitors),
  variables = study_variables, outputs = list(
  counts = omop_output("counts", rows = "visitors", format = "wide", columns = "visits"),
  dictionary = omop_output("dictionary", rows = "visitors", format = "dictionary",
    options = list(source_outputs = "counts"))), publish = "dictionary")
recipe_execute(dictionary, out = c(dictionary = "D_fmt_dictionary"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_dictionary", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_dictionary in site`
#> [1] 2 6
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_dictionary in combined studies`
#> [1] 2 6
```

The two dictionary rows describe the two visit-setting concepts, not patients
or frequencies. A dictionary does not certify that a concept occurred in a particular person, and it is not a replacement for the sparse covariate reference.

## Joined: combine private outputs

A native joined output combines declared output dependencies, using their
protected keys and a checked cardinality. It is not an arbitrary database join.
Keep input columns disjoint and state how many rows can match.


``` r
joined <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits), populations = list(visitors),
  variables = study_variables, outputs = list(
  counts = omop_output("counts", rows = "visitors", format = "wide", columns = "visits"),
  ages = omop_output("ages", rows = "visitors", format = "wide", columns = "age"),
  joined = omop_output("joined", rows = "visitors", format = "joined",
    options = list(from = list(list(output = "counts"), list(output = "ages")),
      how = "left", cardinality = "one_to_one"))), publish = "joined")
```

Only the final joined output is published. The two input outputs are private
intermediate steps and do not each need a separately published symbol.


``` r
joined_result <- recipe_execute(joined, out = c(joined = "D_fmt_joined"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_fmt_joined", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_joined in site`
#> [1] 28  5
#> 
#> $`dimensions of D_fmt_joined in combined studies`
#> [1] 28  5
```

The joined table retains 28 rows. A left join retains the first input's rows. Here each episode has exactly one
counts row and one ages row. Repeated event rows would require a different,
explicit cardinality; do not silently multiply a study population.

## A codebook for every published component

Save the result of `recipe_execute()` to retain metadata about the assigned
objects. The sparse result contains more than one table: its data and its
reference components each have their own schema and row meaning.


``` r
books <- c(recipe_codebook(wide_result), recipe_codebook(sparse_result),
  recipe_codebook(joined_result))
do.call(rbind, lapply(books, function(x) data.frame(
  Output = x$output, Component = x$component, Status = x$status,
  Grain = x$row_grain, Columns = nrow(x$columns))))
```



|                    |Output |Component    |Status    |Grain   | Columns|
|:-------------------|:------|:------------|:---------|:-------|-------:|
|wide/wide           |wide   |wide         |published |episode |       6|
|sparse/sparse       |sparse |sparse       |published |episode |       5|
|sparse/covariateRef |sparse |covariateRef |published |none    |       5|
|joined/joined       |joined |joined       |published |episode |       5|

This is a local metadata operation. It does not count patient rows. Use the same
call for long, period, survival or interval results; multi-component outputs
return one entry per published table.

Inspect the sparse reference table's column types:


``` r
sparse_books <- recipe_codebook(sparse_result)
reference_key <- grep("covariateRef$", names(sparse_books), value = TRUE)
sparse_books[[reference_key]]$columns[c("name", "r_type")]
```



|name         |r_type    |
|:------------|:---------|
|covariate_id |integer   |
|source       |character |
|concept_id   |factor    |
|concept_name |character |
|analysis     |character |

The covariate reference describes feature identities. It is distinct from the
matrix of private person-linked values and from an observed-frequency table.
Read `r_type` as the R representation: text descriptions are character columns.

## Try it

Summarise the visit-count column of the joined output. Why is it the same as the wide count?

<details><summary>Solution</summary>


``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_fmt_joined$visits", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>        5%       10%       25%       50%       75%       90%       95%      Mean 
#>  11.75000  16.40000  23.75000  45.00000  75.25000 117.60000 152.20000  61.96429
```

The mean is 61.96 visits per person across 28 people. Both outputs use the
same reducer and episodes. Joining one row to one row adds a column without duplicating those counts.

</details>

## Another numeric exercise

Summarise the person-level hemoglobin mean in the wide output. Would an average
of a long table's measurement rows give each person equal weight?

<details><summary>Solution</summary>


``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_fmt_wide$hemoglobin", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#> 12.90500 13.14667 13.78500 14.32500 15.33542 15.70000 15.92375 14.46679
```

The overall mean is 14.47 g/dL across 28 person-level means. The wide table
gives each included person one mean in g/dL. An average over
measurement rows would give more weight to people with more measurements.
[Working with lab values](book-14-labs.html) builds this distinction into a
two-connection analysis. Neither shape grants access to individual rows.

</details>

[Chapter 16](book-16-longitudinal.html) develops these choices through irregular
measurements, server reshaping, a discrete-time hazard and pooled mixed models.

## Recap

Choose the population and row meaning before the format. Outputs stay private; multi-component outputs carry reference companions. Censoring and join cardinality are study decisions.

**Next:** [9. Dates, periods and ages](book-09-dates.html).
